newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Analysts cautiously bullish on Malaysia telecoms.
newsitem.headline: Analysts cautiously bullish on Malaysia telecoms.

text.p: Despite fears that intense competition in Malaysia's telecommunications industry will cripple margins and run players out of business, analysts are cautiously bullish.
With consolidations, "at least the industry is on the right track", said Shamsul Shamsudin, telecommunications analyst at brokers Pesaka Jardine Fleming in Kuala Lumpur.
There are seven operators licensed to provide fixed-line services, five licensees for international gateway services, and six mobile telephony operators.
Many feared that for a country with a population of just 20 million, the level of competition would see margins crashing and companies going down with them.

"This would be the case, but several operators are now looking beyond Malaysia's shores to ensure they get enough business," said Phuah Lee Kerk, telecommunications analyst at Vickers Ballas in Kuala Lumpur.
Technology Resources Industries Bhd (TRI) and Mutiara Telecommunications Sdn Bhd are doing this by forming alliances with global players Deutsche Telekom and Swiss Telecom PTT, respectively.
The moves should help TRI and Mutiara make Malaysia an important telecommunications hub for Southeast Asia.

"Using the international gateways in Malaysia, foreign companies like Deutsche Telekom and Swiss Telecom could be able to route their international calls to and from this region through Malaysia," said Phuah.

In July, the Malaysian government reversed its former stance of forcing telecommunications companies to merge. Instead it adopted a policy of allowing market forces to dictate how many companies would merge.

In June, Telekom Malaysia Bhd bought Malaysian Resources Corporation Bhd's (MRCB) subsidiary MRCB Telecommunications Sdn Bhd for 640 million ringgit ($256 million), forming the first alliance between two major industry players within Malaysia.

Also in July, Time Engineering Bhd announced plans to acquire digital mobile operator Sapura Digital Sdn Bhd for 1.2 billion ringgit. Sapura Digital is a wholly owned subsidiary of Sapura Telecommunications Bhd.
There seem to be as many views on the fate of the telecommunications industry in Malaysia as there are analysts studying it.

While Phuah is putting a "neutral" weighting on the sector as a whole, Shamsul at Pesaka Jardine has an "overweight" rating on it, and another analyst, Soon Teck Onn of research house ING Barings, has an "underweight" rating.

The penetration rate for fixed line telephones in Malaysia is only around 16.7 percent, according to government statistics. Several developing countries have penetration rates approaching 50 percent, and this fact alone has spurred foreign investors to invest heavily in the sector, despite the risks.
But some analysts feel some rationalising is inevitable in the industry and that there will be casualties.

"The telecoms industry is going to face cut-throat competition in the coming years," said John Engle, managing director of research house HG Asia in Kuala Lumpur. "As a sector, it will probably underperform the market," he added.
In a report, HG advised clients to sell the stock of privatised Telekom Malaysia and buy TRI. The report said TRI's interim earnings were on track to meet analysts estimates.
Other analysts were also sceptical of Telekom Malaysia's ability to outperform the industry in terms of its earnings.
"Telekom Malaysia is going to lose market share to the other operators quite substantially," said Soon.

"Even though their losses should be mitigated by the government's Universal Services Obligation (USO) which will force the smaller operators to share the provision of some unprofitable services, it will still probably not be enough," he added. The USO should be in place by 1999. ($1 = 2.5 ringgit)
